title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 96
paragraphs: When the sacrifices were favorable to the Greeks, they put their ships to sea from Delos to go to Samos; and arriving off Calamisa in Samos, they moored their ships there opposite the temple of Hera at this place and made preparations for a sea-fight. But the Persians, informed that they were sailing there, also put out to sea and went over to the mainland with their remaining ships (the Phoenician ships having already been sent home). On deliberating, they had thought it good not to fight a battle at sea, since they did not think themselves a match for the enemy; and they sailed away to the mainland so as to be under the protection of their land-army at Mycale, a body that had stayed behind the rest of the army by Xerxes's command, keeping watch over Ionia. Its number was sixty thousand, and its commander was Tigranes, who in beauty and stature surpassed the other Persians. The fleet's commanders, then, had decided to take refuge under this army's protection, draw their ships up on shore, and build an enclosure around them as a protection for the ships and a refuge for themselves.
